transcript:
MEETING: Helix Financial - Security review (Private DR backups: encryption, key ownership, audit evidence)
Recorded: Dec 16, 2025 9:42 AM PT
Duration: 52 minutes

Attendees
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference)
- Marcus Lin (Redwood Inference)
- Olga Petrov (Redwood Inference)
- Hanae Suzuki (Redwood Inference)
- Colin O'Donnell (Redwood Inference)
- Priya Desai (Helix)
- Tom Alvarez (Helix)
- Mei Chen (Helix)
- Nate Brooks (Helix)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Helix asked how Redwood Private backups are encrypted, who owns the keys, and what evidence can be produced for SOC 2 / ISO-aligned controls.
- Redwood explained encryption in transit (TLS), encryption at rest for storage targets (e.g., S3 SSE-KMS), and optional envelope encryption for backup bundles; Redwood does not require access to customer KMS keys.
- Helix emphasized auditability: who initiated backup/restore, immutability/WORM, checksum/integrity, and log retention + SIEM export.
- Next steps include sharing a security FAQ, an evidence bundle example, and confirming Helix backup target + Object Lock requirements.

Topics
1) Backup artifact format + integrity (checksums, manifests)
2) Encryption model (at-rest, in-transit, optional client-side)
3) Key ownership and rotation expectations (KMS/HSM)
4) Restore authorization and break-glass patterns
5) Audit logging + evidence for SOC2/ISO and internal controls

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood to provide written key-handling boundaries and evidence bundle example.
- Helix to confirm storage backend and immutability requirements.

Transcript
[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, I think we’re good to start. Thanks everyone for making time. The goal today is the security review specifically on backup encryption and the evidence you all need for SOC 2 and ISO. I’ve got Marcus from Security Eng, Olga from Compliance, and Hanae who’s been working with the Private packaging side on secrets and cert handling.

[00:18] Priya Desai: Great. And just to level set, we’re evaluating Redwood Private for a regulated workload. Our big gating items are, one, who owns keys for backups; two, audit trail for backup and restore operations; and three, evidence we can show auditors that the controls actually operate.

[00:36] Tom Alvarez: Yeah, and we’ve been burned before where “encrypted” meant something fuzzy. We want details: algorithm, where keys live, and whether a vendor can decrypt.

[00:46] Markus Klein: Totally fair. Marcus, do you want to start with a high-level and then we’ll go deeper?

[00:52] Marcus Lin: Sure. So for Redwood Private backup/restore toolkit, think of it as two layers. Layer one is how we store artifacts in the backup target—S3, MinIO, NFS, etc.—and we support encryption at rest using whatever that backend provides, like SSE-KMS on S3. Layer two is optional encryption of the backup bundle itself before it ever leaves the cluster, using envelope encryption. And in all cases transport is TLS.

[01:20] Mei Chen: When you say “optional,” is it optional for all customers or it’s optional because some environments can’t support it?

[01:27] Marcus Lin: It’s optional because some customers prefer to rely on the storage backend encryption plus tight IAM, and some want the defense-in-depth of encrypting the bundle prior to upload, especially if they’re landing in a shared object store or staging repository. For regulated profiles we usually recommend enabling it.

[01:47] Priya Desai: We’ll likely want it. We also need key ownership to be customer-controlled. Like, we own the KMS key, period.

[01:56] Marcus Lin: That’s the intended model. For S3 + KMS: you create and own the KMS key, you own the IAM policy. Redwood Private components assume an IAM role in your account / environment that has “encrypt/decrypt” permissions as needed, but Redwood (the company) doesn’t hold the key material.

[02:16] Tom Alvarez: But Redwood engineers could, in theory, assume that role if they had access? That’s what we want to avoid.

[02:24] Markus Klein: Yep, understood. In the Private deployment we’re not sitting in the path. Access is under your control. Practically, there are two patterns we see. One: Helix only—your SREs—have that role and Redwood never touches it. Two: a break-glass role exists that can be granted temporarily with approvals for a game day or incident. But it’s your process.

[02:48] Priya Desai: We do have break-glass, but it’s dual approval and fully logged. If you’re going to recommend that, we need to see how it’s audited.

[02:57] Marcus Lin: Makes sense. For AWS specifically, it’s CloudTrail for role assumption and KMS usage logs. For the toolkit itself, we emit structured events and metrics when a backup starts, completes, fails, and when restore enters maintenance mode, etc.

[03:16] Nate Brooks: Can we talk about the artifact format? Integrity matters. We’ve had partial uploads that looked “successful” until restore.

[03:24] Hanae Suzuki: Yeah. The bundle is created with a manifest. It includes checksums per component—DB dump, config snapshot, policy data, and any object-store-copied artifacts—and the upload is done in a way that’s resumable for S3/minio adapters. Then verify checks the manifest and checksums and flags partials.

[03:45] Mei Chen: Is it like a tarball? Or multiple files?

[03:49] Hanae Suzuki: Most deployments use multiple chunk files plus a manifest, because single tarballs get ugly at large sizes. The docs call it a “bundle,” but it’s like: metadata JSON, checksums, and compressed chunks.

[04:04] Tom Alvarez: JSON manifest—does that itself get signed? We care about tampering.

[04:10] Marcus Lin: Today, integrity is primarily the checksums plus immutability controls in the storage backend. If you require cryptographic signing, we can support signing the manifest with a customer-held key, but that’s not the default in the GA baseline.

[04:26] Priya Desai: We might require WORM, object lock, that sort of thing. At least for monthly snapshots.

[04:32] Markus Klein: We can support that on the storage side. We won’t manage it for you, but the toolkit works fine with buckets that have Object Lock or retention policies. We should note restore workflows then need a separate path for “copy to restore location” instead of mutating locked objects.

[04:53] Mei Chen: Okay. Let’s go into encryption. At rest: if we use S3 SSE-KMS with our key. In transit: TLS to S3 endpoints. For the “bundle encryption” you mentioned—what’s the crypto?

[05:07] Marcus Lin: Envelope encryption. Practically: generate a data key per backup, use symmetric encryption like AES-256-GCM for the bundle chunks, then wrap the data key with your KMS key. The wrapped key is stored alongside the backup metadata. On restore, the process calls KMS to unwrap.

[05:31] Tom Alvarez: And Redwood never sees the plaintext data key?

[05:34] Marcus Lin: The running process in your cluster sees it in memory because it must encrypt/decrypt, but Redwood as a vendor doesn’t get it. If Redwood personnel don’t have access to your cluster and don’t have IAM, we can’t retrieve it.

[05:49] Tom Alvarez: Okay, but then it’s about operational boundaries. Our concern is vendor support sessions. People screen share, copy logs, etc.

[05:59] Hanae Suzuki: Yep. We redact. The tooling is designed not to print secrets or plaintext keys. Logs include references like “KMS key ARN used” and “encryption enabled: true,” but not the data key. Also the config schema supports marking fields as sensitive so the CLI outputs “REDACTED.”

[06:20] Priya Desai: That’s helpful. We need an explicit statement, for procurement, that Redwood personnel do not have access to customer-managed keys and do not require it for support.

[06:30] Markus Klein: We can provide that in writing. Marcus can draft the technical language.

[06:35] Marcus Lin: Yep.

[06:38] Nate Brooks: How about database backups? This is Postgres? Are you using pg_dump or some snapshotting?

[06:44] Hanae Suzuki: For control plane DB, default is pg_dump for the logical backup, plus optional WAL archiving for point-in-time restore. The tooling can coordinate putting the system in a quiesced state via maintenance mode so writes are blocked during the critical window.

[07:03] Mei Chen: Maintenance mode is at the app layer, not Postgres locks, right?

[07:08] Hanae Suzuki: Right, it’s control plane services rejecting write paths and waiting for inflight. It reduces lock contention. It’s not perfect for every integration but it’s the supported path.

[07:21] Tom Alvarez: Evidence: we need to show that backups ran on schedule, that they were encrypted, and that restores were tested. What artifacts do you produce that are auditor-friendly?

[07:33] Olga Petrov: I can take that. For evidence, we usually recommend a bundle that includes: (1) backup job logs showing start/finish timestamps and backup ID, (2) verification output showing checksum pass and encryption enabled, (3) object store inventory listing for the backup prefix with retention settings, (4) change management ticket link for restore drills, and (5) restore drill runbook with sign-off and measured RTO.

[07:59] Priya Desai: That’s the kind of thing we need. Do you have a template?

[08:03] Olga Petrov: Yes, we have a DR drill template used internally and for customers. It captures scenario, timeline, RTO/RPO, commands run, and follow-ups. We can share a version that’s customer-facing.

[08:18] Tom Alvarez: For SOC2, we also want access controls around who can initiate restore. Restore is the scary one.

[08:25] Marcus Lin: Agree. Restore should be tightly permissioned. In Kubernetes terms, the restore job runs under a service account with elevated permissions, but you can gate who can create that job via RBAC, and in some environments we integrate with an approval workflow. From the cloud side, the IAM role used for KMS decrypt can be separate from encrypt, and can require MFA or be break-glass.

[08:52] Mei Chen: That’s important. We’d prefer separate roles: backup role can encrypt and write, restore role can decrypt and read, but only assumed under break-glass.

[09:02] Hanae Suzuki: That’s supported. The adapters support separate credentials for backup and restore. The Helm chart values can mount different secrets, and the CLI can reference different profiles.

[09:13] Tom Alvarez: Does the product require storing any credentials inside your control plane DB?

[09:18] Hanae Suzuki: We recommend not storing cloud credentials in the DB. It’s Kubernetes secrets / external secret manager integration. The backup toolkit will reference secrets mounted into the job.

[09:30] Priya Desai: External secret manager—Vault, cloud secret manager?

[09:34] Hanae Suzuki: Yes. Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, etc. We don’t ship Vault; we just support reading from Kubernetes secrets or external-secrets patterns.

[09:44] Tom Alvarez: Competitors… sorry to bring it up… we use Velero in some clusters. Why not just use that?

[09:51] Markus Klein: Fair question. Velero is great for cluster resources, PV snapshots, etc. Our experience is it doesn’t cover application-level sequencing for our control plane and doesn’t cover policy/config services in a consistent way, especially for on-prem and air-gapped. Our toolkit is opinionated around Redwood’s state inventory and restore gates.

[10:13] Nate Brooks: The restore gates sound key. What are you checking?

[10:17] Hanae Suzuki: After restore, it runs health checks: control plane API up, DB schema matches expected version, policy service loads, and then smoke tests against the private endpoints. If critical checks fail, it stops and tells operator what to do; it doesn’t “declare success” prematurely.

[10:36] Mei Chen: Any risk that health checks leak data to logs? Like, do you log sample prompts?

[10:42] Hanae Suzuki: No prompts. The smoke tests are basic, like a version endpoint, auth handshake, and a minimal request that doesn’t persist customer data. Logs are structured and redact payloads where applicable.

[10:57] Tom Alvarez: We also need audit logs. Specifically: who did what and when. For example: “entered maintenance mode” and “restore executed” should be recorded.

[11:08] Marcus Lin: Yes. There are multiple layers: Kubernetes audit logs for who created jobs, CloudTrail for IAM role assumptions and KMS decrypt calls, application logs for maintenance mode transitions and backup/restore events. We can export control plane events to your SIEM via your existing log pipeline.

[11:29] Priya Desai: Can you produce an audit log that’s human readable without us stitching together three systems?

[11:35] Markus Klein: We can provide a recommended “evidence packet” process so it’s a repeatable export. But in a Private deployment, we can’t centralize your cloud provider logs. We can help you set up dashboards and an operator checklist.

[11:52] Priya Desai: That’s okay, as long as the checklist is crisp and auditors can follow it.

[12:00] Olga Petrov: We can align it to your internal controls language. If you share your control IDs, we’ll map: backup frequency, verification, access restrictions, and restore testing.

[12:12] Tom Alvarez: One more: key rotation. Do you assume keys rotate? How does that impact old backups?

[12:20] Marcus Lin: For KMS keys, rotation is supported. Old backups encrypted under older key versions remain decryptable as long as the key is enabled and the policy allows. If you re-encrypt or move to a new key, that’s on the storage side or via a rewrap process.

[12:38] Mei Chen: We have a policy that keys can’t be disabled without a documented impact analysis. So we’d keep them.

[12:45] Marcus Lin: That’s consistent.

[12:47] Nate Brooks: Air-gapped might come later for us, but we have a subsidiary that is basically offline. Does your approach work there?

[12:56] Hanae Suzuki: In air-gapped, storage targets are usually on-prem object store or NFS. We support a local file bundle and “staging repository” mounted into the cluster. For keys, we’ve seen HSM integrations where key unwrap happens via local KMS/HSM, but we’ll need to understand your environment.

[13:18] Tom Alvarez: In that case, no cloud KMS. So the “wrap” step needs to use our HSM.

[13:24] Marcus Lin: Right. The interface is “key provider.” Cloud KMS is one provider. HSM can be another. We’d validate compatibility in a pilot.

[13:35] Priya Desai: For this initial deal, we’re focusing on AWS VPC, not on-prem.

[13:41] Markus Klein: Great.

[13:43] (crosstalk)

[13:44] Priya Desai: Sorry, go ahead Tom.

[13:46] Tom Alvarez: Logging redaction: do you log bucket names, account IDs, or ARNs? Those are sometimes considered sensitive.

[13:54] Hanae Suzuki: Bucket names and ARNs can appear, yes, because they’re required to troubleshoot AccessDenied. But we can make that configurable. We do not log object contents, nor do we log secrets. And we can ensure PII isn’t in logs.

[14:11] Tom Alvarez: Fine, we just need it documented.

[14:14] Olga Petrov: Also for evidence: some customers prefer screenshots of the dashboard showing “last successful backup age” and “backup success rate” plus the runbook link. That’s sometimes enough for auditors.

[14:27] Priya Desai: We prefer exports, not screenshots, but we can do both.

[14:31] Markus Klein: Understood.

[14:33] Mei Chen: Can we talk about retention and pruning? If the toolkit prunes backups, we need controls so it doesn’t delete the “last known good” one.

[14:42] Hanae Suzuki: Yes, there’s safety logic: it won’t delete the latest verified snapshot, and it has an idempotent behavior. Pruning uses retention policy—like keep daily for 14 days, weekly for 8 weeks, monthly for 12 months—configurable.

[15:00] Nate Brooks: Does pruning honor object lock? If objects are immutable, delete will fail.

[15:05] Hanae Suzuki: Correct. In that case it errors with a clear message and suggests adjusting retention policy or using a different prefix. The job surfaces a “prune failed due to retention lock” metric so you can alert.

[15:20] Tom Alvarez: Metrics: you said metrics are emitted. What’s the label set? We don’t want secrets in labels.

[15:27] Hanae Suzuki: Labels are like cluster ID, environment, backup type, result. Not bucket names or object keys.

[15:36] Tom Alvarez: Okay.

[15:38] Priya Desai: Let’s be explicit: does Redwood ever have access to plaintext backup data?

[15:44] Marcus Lin: Not by default. In Private deployments, backups live in your storage and are encrypted under your keys. Redwood the company does not receive copies. If you choose to share a backup with us for troubleshooting, that would be a separate customer action and we’d recommend you redact or use a non-production dataset.

[16:03] Priya Desai: We will not share prod backups.

[16:05] Markus Klein: Makes sense.

[16:07] Tom Alvarez: Another one: during restore, you mentioned maintenance mode that blocks writes. Is that auditable? Like, can we show “writes were rejected” and “maintenance mode enabled”?

[16:19] Hanae Suzuki: Yes. Control plane emits events when maintenance mode toggles, and API write calls get rejected with an explicit error. Those events can be logged.

[16:31] Tom Alvarez: We may need that as evidence in post-incident writeups.

[16:35] Olga Petrov: We can incorporate that into the restore drill template. There’s a checklist line: “Maintenance mode enabled; verify write-path rejection observed.”

[16:48] Priya Desai: Good.

[16:50] Markus Klein: Can we shift to what you’ll need to approve the vendor? Priya, can you list the artifacts?

[16:56] Priya Desai: Sure. We need: (1) statement on key ownership and no vendor access; (2) encryption details for backups; (3) audit log sources and how to export; (4) sample runbook and evidence checklist; and (5) confirmation of role separation for backup vs restore.

[17:16] Markus Klein: Great.

[17:18] Marcus Lin: I’ll add: we should specify encryption in transit (TLS 1.2+), and for S3 SSE-KMS it’s AES-256 under the hood, and for envelope encryption AES-256-GCM. We’ll write it cleanly.

[17:35] Tom Alvarez: Please include whether you support customer-provided keys only, or if you ever require Redwood-managed keys.

[17:42] Marcus Lin: For Private: customer-managed. For hosted API: Redwood-managed. But this deal is Private.

[17:49] Priya Desai: Good distinction.

[17:51] Mei Chen: I’d like IAM examples. Specifically least privilege: bucket prefix, KMS key policy, and the “deny delete” except for pruning job maybe.

[18:03] Markus Klein: We have examples. We’ll send. Also we can do a separate session with your infra team to tailor.

[18:10] Mei Chen: Great.

[18:12] (brief pause)

[18:14] Nate Brooks: Restore testing frequency. For ISO, we test at least annually; we prefer quarterly. What do you recommend?

[18:22] Olga Petrov: We recommend quarterly restore drills for strict tier, semi-annual for standard tier, depending on your RTO/RPO requirements and appetite. The tooling is designed to make drills less painful.

[18:37] Priya Desai: Okay.

[18:39] Tom Alvarez: I want to make sure we’re not missing secrets and certificates. Are they in the backup? If yes, how are they protected?

[18:47] Hanae Suzuki: Good callout. By default we do NOT include Kubernetes secrets in a general-purpose backup unless you explicitly opt in. Certificates can be handled in two ways: regenerate from your CA during restore, or back up cert material encrypted. Many customers prefer regenerate. The runbooks call out the dependency.

[19:11] Tom Alvarez: So if you don’t back up secrets, restore might fail because a secret is missing.

[19:17] Hanae Suzuki: Correct, which is why the “restore plan” step enumerates prerequisites and flags missing secret sources. It basically says, “you need to re-provision these secrets from Vault” etc.

[19:30] Priya Desai: That’s good; we prefer no secrets in backups.

[19:34] Markus Klein: And for evidence, we can show that policy—secrets excluded—so auditors don’t get nervous.

[19:41] Tom Alvarez: Nice.

[19:43] Mei Chen: What about logs? Are logs part of the backup?

[19:47] Hanae Suzuki: Not typically, except the backup job logs for evidence. Platform logs are usually in your logging system and have separate retention.

[19:55] Nate Brooks: Okay.

[19:57] Markus Klein: We’ve covered the big items. Any remaining concerns?

[20:02] Tom Alvarez: The big one is: we need a clear boundary statement. “Redwood does not have access to customer data, backups, or keys in Private deployment.” Something like that.

[20:12] Marcus Lin: We can do that, with nuance: we don’t have access unless you explicitly grant us access. That’s the accurate statement.

[20:20] Priya Desai: Yep, that’s fine.

[20:22] (timestamp drift; transcript skips ahead)

[27:11] Mei Chen: Sorry, quick follow-up on KMS. If we use VPC endpoints only, no public internet, does your backup job support that?

[27:20] Hanae Suzuki: Yes. That’s common. The S3 adapter supports VPC endpoints; you just configure the endpoint and ensure DNS/resolution. Same for KMS endpoint.

[27:34] Mei Chen: Great.

[27:35] Tom Alvarez: And if KMS is cross-account? We have a centralized security account.

[27:42] Marcus Lin: That’s doable but often trips on key policy. We’ll provide a known-good example and the common pitfalls. The main thing is ensuring the role in the workload account can use the key in the security account with an explicit allow.

[28:02] Priya Desai: Please include that in the IAM examples.

[28:05] Markus Klein: Will do.

[28:07] (crosstalk)

[28:08] Nate Brooks: Does the toolkit support “test restore” without impacting prod? Like restore into a separate cluster.

[28:15] Hanae Suzuki: Yes, there’s a “restore to new cluster” flow. It’s the recommended way to drill without touching prod. You restore control plane first, validate, and only then cut over DNS if it’s an actual disaster scenario.

[28:32] Nate Brooks: Perfect.

[28:34] Priya Desai: For evidence, a successful drill report is critical.

[28:38] Olga Petrov: We’ll share the template.

[28:40] (transcription note: speaker labels may be incorrect)

[35:09] Erin Walsh: Hi, sorry I joined late. Procurement question: does any of this require additional licensing? Like the backup toolkit.

[35:17] Markus Klein: It’s part of the Private packaging. Some advanced observability retention is an add-on, but backup/restore tooling is included.

[35:26] Erin Walsh: Okay.

[35:27] Priya Desai: We’re almost done. Markus, can you recap deliverables?

[35:33] Markus Klein: Yep. We’ll send (1) a security FAQ / statement on key ownership and access boundaries, (2) encryption details for backup bundles, (3) IAM least-privilege examples including cross-account KMS and separate backup vs restore roles, (4) the DR drill template and a sanitized example evidence packet.

[35:56] Tom Alvarez: And documentation for log redaction and what’s in logs.

[35:59] Markus Klein: Yes, add that.

[36:01] Marcus Lin: I’ll include the logging section—what we log, what we don’t.

[36:06] Priya Desai: Timeline: we want to complete security review by end of next week.

[36:12] Markus Klein: That works. We can get most of this to you tomorrow, and the mapping to your control IDs by end of week if you share those IDs.

[36:22] Priya Desai: I’ll send them.

[36:25] Olga Petrov: Great.

[36:27] Markus Klein: Any last questions?

[36:30] Mei Chen: None from me.

[36:32] Tom Alvarez: All good. Thanks.

[36:34] Markus Klein: Thanks everyone.

(End of transcript)

Notes
- Several mentions of “bundle encryption” refer to optional envelope encryption for backup artifacts in addition to storage-backend encryption.
- Helix emphasized auditor-facing evidence and role separation for restore operations.
